vignette:
He is a 78-year-old African man who has spent much of his life in libraries, surrounded by quiet, order, and the steady comfort of books that remain where they are placed. He speaks of himself as a husband first and as a librarian second, someone who has always believed that careful work and routine can hold the world together. That belief is shaken the day terrorists attack the district where he lives and works.

He describes the event in fragments, as if his memory still moves around the edges of it. The morning begins like any other. He is at the library, checking returns and helping a student find a history text, when the first explosion sounds in the distance. At first he thinks it is construction or a generator failing, something ordinary and explainable. Then the windows tremble. People look up. Someone runs through the reading room shouting that armed men are nearby. He remembers the sudden change in the air, the way the building that had always seemed so solid becomes a place with no safety in it. He drops to the floor with others, pressing his body against the shelves, listening for footsteps, gunfire, screams. He thinks of his wife immediately, then of their grandchildren, then of whether he will ever again see the morning light in his home.

For hours, he is trapped in fear and confusion, waiting while the violence continues outside. Even after he is able to leave, the world feels rearranged. Streets he has known for decades seem strange and dangerous. He returns home shaken, but not relieved. His wife is alive, and that fact should calm him, yet he is unable to settle into gratitude. Instead, he watches the doors and windows, starts at every sound, and keeps listening for the next explosion. In the days that follow, he sleeps lightly or not at all. When he does drift off, he wakes with his heart racing, certain he has heard shouting or the crack of gunfire. He begins keeping a light on through the night, saying it is for his wife’s comfort, though it is really for his own.

Before the attack, he had been a man of routine: early rising, careful dress, breakfast with his wife, then the library, where he enjoyed stamping books, shelving them in order, and assisting students who approached him with respect. Afterward, he used to walk home at an unhurried pace, carrying small stories from the day. Now he avoids the route near the library because it brings back the smell of smoke and the sound of broken glass. He has not been able to return to full work. When he does enter the building, he feels disoriented, as if the quiet is false and another attack is waiting just beyond hearing. He scans the entrances and sits facing the door. He no longer trusts crowds, and he keeps close to walls when he must move through public places. He has stopped attending community gatherings he once enjoyed, telling friends he is too old, though privately he knows he cannot tolerate the feeling of being exposed.

He notices changes in himself that trouble him. He is more irritable with his wife, then ashamed of his sharpness. He becomes tense over minor noises—a dropped pan, a motorcycle backfiring, a door slamming in the street. He speaks less, especially about the attack, because the moment he begins to tell it, the images return too vividly and he feels as though he is back on the floor of the library with his body locked in place. Sometimes he avoids television news entirely; other times he watches in a grim, compelled way, as if needing to know what danger is coming next. He carries a persistent sense that the world is unsafe and that he failed to protect those around him. This weighs on him particularly as a husband and elder, roles he has always associated with steadiness and provision.

At night, he often sits awake beside his wife, listening to the house settle. He thinks about mortality more than he once did, not in an abstract way but with the practical fear that death can arrive suddenly and indiscriminately. He mourns the version of himself who moved through the world without scanning for threats. Yet there are moments when he still goes to the library, straightens a row of books, and feels for a brief time the familiar logic of order. In those moments he seems to reach toward the man he was before the attack, even as the memory of that day remains close, intruding into ordinary hours and shaping the way he moves through each one now.
